OU art professor explores the meaning of Rome’s “Great Mosaic”

Dania Neiroukh, Arts Reporter
September 23, 2026
Photo courtesy of Cody VanderKaay
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:04
Instaread

A colossal Roman mosaic that remained hidden for centuries is now open to the public, offering a new look into the art and culture of ancient Rome.

The ancient work was first discovered in the 1990s during excavations inside the Baths of Trajan in Rome. After years of excavation and restoration, the mosaic recently opened to the public alongside the “Painted City” fresco.

The Great Mosaic is approximately 33 feet high and 52 feet wide, with additional sections still being uncovered. It contains architectural designs, human figures and views of a maritime city.

The nearby “Painted City” fresco depicts a city from above, showing buildings, towers, a theater, a temple and public spaces. Researchers still do not know whether the city shown was a real location or an imagined one.

For Cody VanderKaay, Oakland University Associate Professor of Art and Art Program Director, the size of the Great Mosaic is one of the most important parts of understanding the work.

“What strikes me first is that scale is never just a matter of making something bigger,” VanderKaay said. “Scale becomes part of the meaning of the work.”

According to VanderKaay, viewing something this large creates an entirely different experience than viewing a smaller piece of art. Instead of looking at the artwork from one position, the viewer has to physically move around to understand it.

“Your body becomes involved in the experience — you have to move, look, step back, get closer and take in different parts of the work over time,” VanderKaay said.

VanderKaay also discusses the importance of scale with his students at OU. In his “Small Works” course, students consider how making something larger or smaller can change the relationship between an artwork and the person viewing it.

“A small object can ask us to lean in and pay attention; a very large work can surround us or overwhelm us,” VanderKaay said.

The size of the Great Mosaic also gives insight into how much work would have gone into creating it. A piece this large required more than artistic talent; it also required planning, materials, time and the cooperation of many people.

“With an ancient work like the Great Mosaic, I also find myself thinking about the coordination of labor,” VanderKaay said. “Even if we don’t know the identity of every person involved, the finished work is evidence of an organized process involving materials, specialized knowledge, exchange, time and human labor and interaction.”

For VanderKaay, studying this process can tell us more about the society responsible for creating the work. The amount of time and resources devoted to art can reveal what people considered important enough to preserve and display.

“The imagery and subject matter can tell us something about what people valued, believed, admired or wanted to communicate,” VanderKaay said.

The location of the mosaic is another important part of experiencing it. Unlike an artwork that has been removed from its original location and displayed in a museum, the Great Mosaic remains connected to the architecture and environment surrounding it.

“A mosaic installed as part of architecture isn’t experienced in the same way that a mosaic hanging on a museum wall is,” VanderKaay said. “Its location, surrounding architecture, light, scale and relationship to the viewer all contribute to its meaning.”

Although almost 2,000 years separate modern artists from the people responsible for the mosaic, VanderKaay believes many of the ideas behind creating art have remained similar.

“I think ancient art matters a great deal because it reminds us that people thousands of years ago were thinking about many of the same fundamental things that artists think about today: identity, power, beauty, mortality, memory, storytelling, status, the natural world and our relationship to one another,” he said.

The Great Mosaic survived long after the people who worked on it, allowing their decisions and ideas to still be studied today.

“An artwork can outlive the person who made it and carry the conversation forward,” VanderKaay said.

After thousands of years underground, the Great Mosaic is allowing that conversation to continue.
